passage: Salma has a crush on the debate captain, and I've watched it take over her whole year. She knows his timetable better than her own. She writes his initials inside her geometry box and covers them with a sticker when anyone looks. Every time he speaks at assembly she grips my arm and whispers, "Usha, he's just so kind." Last week, in the canteen line, I saw him snap at the boy who serves tea because the cup was too full. Salma saw it too. On the way back she said, "He must be really stressed with the finals." I didn't argue. I don't know what's really going on in her head. Maybe she knows he isn't perfect and just doesn't want to know yet.

qa.q: What does Salma write inside her geometry box?
qa.a: She writes the debate captain's initials and hides them under a sticker.

qa.q: Why might Salma have explained away the captain snapping at the tea boy?
qa.a: She has built a flawless picture of him in her head, so she seems to want to protect it and quickly finds an excuse rather than feel disappointed.

qa.q: What could Usha do if she wants to help without hurting Salma?
qa.a: She could stay close and keep listening, and gently ask questions about the real boy rather than lecturing or mocking the crush.

qa.q: How is Usha affected by watching her friend's crush?
qa.a: She feels a bit sidelined and worried, and she is unsure what Salma truly thinks, so she chooses silence over a fight.

grounding: An onlooking friend describes a teen's intense, idealised crush that makes her excuse the boy's flaws.

passage:
Monday: A new boy, Asif, joined Chandrika's evening maths tuition. He dropped his pen, grinned, and said sorry to the whole room. Chandrika decided he had the nicest laugh she had ever heard.

Friday: He messaged the tuition group asking for the chapter notes, and she sent them within ten seconds. He replied, "thanks 🙏". She read that one word so many times she knew the exact shape of the emoji. In bed she planned their whole future, down to the colour of their front door.

Three weeks later: Asif still hadn't returned her notebook. When a quieter girl got a sum wrong, he joked about it loudly. Chandrika felt something sink, then oddly loosen. Walking home, she noticed she hadn't checked her phone once.

qa.q: What did Asif ask the tuition group for on Friday?
qa.a: He asked for the chapter notes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she planned their whole future in bed?
qa.a: She was swept up in an intense, dreamy crush, building a perfect story from one short thanks.

qa.q: How could an older sister or friend support Chandrika through this?
qa.a: Listen without teasing, let her enjoy the feelings, and gently remind her that people show who they are slowly, over time.

qa.q: What would change if Asif had returned the notebook and been kind to the quieter girl?
qa.a: Chandrika's idealised picture might have lasted longer, and the letdown, when it came, might have come from something else.

grounding: Traces a teen's idealised crush rising fast and then softening as she sees the real person.

passage: "Jomon, sit. You think no one understands? When I was a girl of fifteen, I was certain I would marry the boy who played guitar at the church youth festival. I never spoke to him properly, mind you. I just watched. I learnt his cousin's name so I could find out his birthday. I wrote him long letters I never posted and kept them under my mattress. When he smiled in my direction once, I didn't eat dinner, I was so full of it. Your grandmother kept asking, "Avni, are you ill?" She thought I had a fever. Years later I met him at a wedding. Nice fellow, very ordinary, talked about tyre prices. I laughed all the way home. The feeling was real, mind you. But the boy in my head was mostly me."

qa.q: Where did the boy Avni liked play the guitar?
qa.a: He played at the church youth festival.

qa.q: What does Avni's skipping dinner after one smile suggest about her feelings at fifteen?
qa.a: She was so overwhelmed and excited by a tiny sign of attention that ordinary things like hunger faded; the crush filled her completely.

qa.q: What could Jomon take from Avni's story about a crush of their own?
qa.a: Jomon can feel it without shame, while remembering that the person he admires may be quite different up close. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jomon feel hearing this story from Avni?
qa.a: Jomon might feel less alone and less embarrassed, because someone he respects admits she went through the same intense feelings.

grounding: An elder recalls her own idealised teenage crush to reassure a younger relative.

passage: The chemistry exam was at nine the next morning, and Devika had read the same page on bonds four times. Her phone lay face-down, but she kept flipping it over to check whether the senior from the quiz club had replied to her 'good luck for the finals' message. He hadn't. In her head he was already perfect: kind to juniors, brilliant, the sort who would remember her birthday. She had spoken to him exactly twice. At ten, Sunaina called to revise. 'Are you even listening?' 'Sorry. Do you think he's the type who reads messages and doesn't reply?' Sunaina sighed. 'Dev, you don't know what type he is. You know his profile picture.' Devika laughed, a little hurt. Then she put the phone in the kitchen and opened the page on bonds again.

qa.q: How many times had Devika spoken to the senior?
qa.a: Exactly twice.

qa.q: What does Devika imagining him as perfect suggest about her crush?
qa.a: Her feelings are built more on her own idealised picture than on actually knowing him.

qa.q: What small step helped Devika at the end, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the kitchen, because it stopped the constant checking so she could study.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Devika's crush?
qa.a: Sunaina sees it as based on very little real knowledge and gently teases her back toward reality.

grounding: Shows a teenager's idealised crush crowding out exam revision the night before a test.

passage: Every day that week, Parul took the long way home through the Jaipur market, past the library where the boy with the sketchbook sat by the window. She had never heard his voice. She had decided he was gentle, that he drew his grandmother, that he probably liked old songs. She filled the back pages of her notebook with his initials beside hers, then scribbled them out. On Friday, Noor walked with her. 'Parul, this is twenty minutes extra. For a window.' 'You don't get it.' 'Try me.' Parul stopped. 'When I think about him, everything else goes quiet.' Noor softened. Then they reached the library. The window seat was empty. Parul's stomach dropped, and the whole walk home she barely spoke.

qa.q: In which city is the market?
qa.a: Jaipur.

qa.q: What did Parul mean by 'everything else goes quiet'?
qa.a: Thinking about the boy gives her an intense, absorbing feeling that crowds out her other worries.

qa.q: How could Noor support Parul without mocking her?
qa.a: Noor could keep walking with Parul sometimes, listen, and gently help her notice how much she has imagined compared with what she knows. 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Parul actually spoke to the boy?
qa.a: Her idealised picture would meet the real person, which might disappoint or surprise her, but it would be real.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's intense, idealised crush on a boy she has never spoken to.

passage:
"Didi, you've drawn his name on your hand again."
"Divyansh, go away."
"Arjit this, Arjit that. What's so special?"
Sarita, fifteen, sighed dreamily. "He's perfect. He helped a stray dog out of the drain. He reads poetry. He has the kindest eyes."
"Have you talked to him?"
"Once. He said 'excuse me' in the corridor."
"That's it?"
"The way he said it, though."
"He also picks his nose in maths."
"He does not!"
"Does. I sit behind him in tuition."
Sarita threw a pillow at him, but she went quiet afterwards, rubbing the ink off her hand.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw on her hand?
qa.a: His name, Arjit.

qa.q: What does Sarita calling Arjit "perfect" after one conversation suggest?
qa.a: She is infatuated, idealising him and filling in the gaps with what she hopes he is.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarita about her crush?
qa.a: It's okay to have strong feelings, but getting to know Arjit as a real person would show who he actually is.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see his sister's crush?
qa.a: He finds it silly and teases her, but his detail makes her think.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense, idealised crush on a boy she barely knows.

passage: I'm Aparna, and at sixteen I was completely sure I was in love with my friend Sonali's older brother. He was in college. He played guitar on their balcony, and I'd find reasons to visit. I wrote pages in my diary about his hands, his laugh, how he'd once handed me a glass of water. I imagined whole conversations. Then one day I heard him arguing with Sonali about who'd finish the milk, just like any brother. I laughed so hard I had to leave. The feeling didn't vanish at once, but I began to see him as a person, not a poster.

qa.q: What did Sonali's brother play on the balcony?
qa.a: Guitar.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel while writing pages about him?
qa.a: Aparna felt swept up and dreamy, full of intense, idealised feelings.

qa.q: What turning point helped Aparna see him more clearly?
qa.a: Hearing him argue with Sonali about milk, which showed he was an ordinary person.

qa.q: How might Sonali have seen Aparna's frequent visits?
qa.a: She might have noticed and been amused, or wondered if she was the real reason Aparna came.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on an idealised crush and the moment it became more realistic.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Sangeeta, February
Kishore (15) has been distracted for two weeks. His notebook margins are full of one girl's initials, and he looks towards the next section whenever the door opens. His friends say he's written her a long letter but won't send it. I didn't mention it directly. I asked how he was, and he said, "I can't think about anything else." I told him strong feelings are normal and asked him to keep one hour a day for study. I'll keep an eye on his marks and check in again next week.

qa.q: What fills Kishore's notebook margins?
qa.a: One girl's initials.

qa.q: What does Kishore saying "I can't think about anything else" suggest?
qa.a: He is infatuated, caught up in intense and consuming feelings.

qa.q: Why was Sangeeta's approach sensible?
qa.a: She respected his privacy, told him the feelings are normal and gave him a simple structure for study.

qa.q: How might Kishore's friends see his unsent letter?
qa.a: They might tease him, or be curious whether he'll ever send it.

grounding: Shows a teenager consumed by an intense crush, noticed by his class teacher.

passage:
Thursday. Nilesh's diary.
Nirmala wore a yellow dupatta to tuition today. I noticed because I notice everything she does. She laughed at something Sir said and tucked her hair behind her ear, and I missed the entire trigonometry problem. I've written her name in the back of my maths notebook eleven times. I imagine us walking home together, talking about books, even though I don't know if she reads. I don't actually know much about her. I've spoken to her twice: once to borrow an eraser, once to say "bye." But in my head she's perfect. Maybe tomorrow I'll say something normal. Like "Did you get the homework?" Ugh. Even that feels terrifying.

qa.q: What colour was Nirmala's dupatta?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about talking to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nilesh feels intensely nervous and excited, even terrified of saying something simple.

qa.q: What could help Nilesh see Nirmala more realistically?
qa.a: Having ordinary conversations with her and getting to know her, rather than imagining her as perfect.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Nilesh?
qa.a: She probably sees Nilesh as a quiet classmate who once borrowed an eraser, unaware of the crush.

grounding: A teen's diary shows an intense, idealised crush on a classmate barely spoken to.

passage: In Sangli, Manoj, fifteen, took the long road home every day, past the flower stall where Urmila helped her aunt after school. He had never spoken to her. But he knew she wore a steel bangle, that she hummed while tying marigolds, and that she laughed with her head back. He'd decided she was kind, clever and brave. At night he wrote her name in the margin of his history notes, then scribbled over it. His friend Salim noticed the detour. "You'll ride past her till the board exams?" Manoj went red. "I'm just taking the long way." "Do you even know what she likes?" Manoj opened his mouth, then closed it. He didn't know a single thing she liked.

qa.q: What does Urmila hum while doing?
qa.a: While tying marigolds.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Salim asked if he knew what she liked?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit shaken, realising he knew almost nothing about her.

qa.q: What could Manoj do if he wants to know Urmila as a real person?
qa.a: He could start a simple, respectful conversation at the stall, and accept however she responds.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Manoj riding past every day?
qa.a: She may not notice him at all, or may find it odd, since he has never spoken to her.

grounding: A small-town teenager idealises a girl he has never spoken to, until a friend's question stops him.

passage:
Zanele had watched the new boy in her Johannesburg maths class, Sipho, for exactly nine days. She knew he drew spirals in the margins, that he laughed silently with his shoulders, that he had a scar on his thumb. She had decided he was kind, brave, secretly a poet.
Her friend Olga sighed at lunch. "You've never spoken to him."
"I don't need to. I just know."
That afternoon he asked Zanele for a pencil. She handed it over with shaking fingers and couldn't speak. He said thanks and turned back.
Later Olga found her writing his name in tiny letters on her ruler. "Zanele. What if he's just a boy who draws spirals?"
Zanele laughed, but for a second, the thought stung.

qa.q: How many days had Zanele watched Sipho?
qa.a: Exactly nine days.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when Sipho asked for a pencil?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and nervous; her fingers shook and she couldn't speak.

qa.q: What could Zanele try if she wants to know Sipho as he really is?
qa.a: She could start a simple conversation, maybe about maths or his drawings, and let the real person replace the picture in her head.

qa.q: How does Olga see Zanele's crush?
qa.a: Olga finds it a bit much and gently worries that Zanele has built up an idea of Sipho without knowing him.

grounding: Shows a teen idealising a crush she barely knows.

passage:
In the school library, Kavitha had been pretending to read the same page for twenty minutes. Two tables away, the senior who ran the astronomy club was sorting slides for his talk.
Her friend Tenzin whispered, "You're doing it again."
"Doing what?"
"Staring. You joined astronomy club for him. You don't even like stars."
"I like stars now." Kavitha's cheeks burned. "He said Jupiter has ninety moons like it was poetry."
"He reads that off a slide, Kavi."
She knew it was silly. She had drawn his handwriting in her rough book, planned what she'd say if he ever asked her a question, and imagined whole conversations on the walk home.
When he looked up and smiled at the whole table, her heart hammered for the entire next period.

qa.q: What did the senior say about Jupiter?
qa.a: That Jupiter has ninety moons, like it was poetry.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when Tenzin said she was staring?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and flustered; her cheeks burned.

qa.q: How could Tenzin support Kavitha kindly?
qa.a: Tenzin could tease gently but also encourage her to enjoy the club for its own sake, not only for the senior.

qa.q: How might the senior see the situation, if at all?
qa.a: He probably has no idea; to him Kavitha may be just another club member at the table.

grounding: Shows a teen building an intense, idealised crush on an older student in a school setting.

passage:
Dear Tushar,
You're the only person I can tell this to, because you're my cousin and you're three cities away.
There's a boy in my tuition class. I've never had a proper conversation with him. But I've memorised his timetable, the colour of his cycle, and the song he hums before tests. I think about him while brushing my teeth. I write things in my diary that I'd die if anyone read.
Yesterday he held the door for me, and I replayed it about fifty times.
Part of me knows I've made him into a movie character. Part of me doesn't care, it feels so good.
Is this normal? Please don't laugh. Actually, you can laugh a little.
Kavitha

qa.q: What does Kavitha say she has memorised about the boy?
qa.a: His timetable, the colour of his cycle, and the song he hums before tests.

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel about this crush?
qa.a: Kavitha feels giddy and a bit embarrassed, knowing she has idealised him but enjoying the feeling anyway.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha if Tushar wrote back asking?
qa.a: Enjoy the feeling but keep her own routines, and get to know the boy as a person before deciding who he is.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Tushar may feel trusted and amused, and a little protective of a cousin who is swept up.

grounding: A teen writes to a cousin about an intense, idealised crush.

passage: Jatin, don't tell anyone, but it's Karthik confessing here: I've been writing her name in the margin of my chemistry book for three weeks. Meenakshi, from tuition. She laughed once at something I said about Sir's tie, and I replayed it for two days. I sit where I can see the door when she comes in. I know she likes filter coffee with extra sugar. In my head she's perfect: kind, funny, never in a bad mood. Yesterday she snapped at her friend over a borrowed pen, and I felt almost cheated, like she'd broken character. Which is silly, right? I barely know her. I think I've fallen for a person I made up.

qa.q: Whose name has Karthik been writing in the margin of the chemistry book?
qa.a: Meenakshi's name, from tuition.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when Meenakshi snapped at her friend?
qa.a: Karthik felt almost cheated and let down, as if the perfect picture had cracked.

qa.q: What could Karthik do to get past the idealised picture?
qa.a: Karthik could get to know Meenakshi as an ordinary person through normal, friendly conversation at tuition, and let the crush become something real or fade.

qa.q: How might Jatin respond to Karthik's confession?
qa.a: Jatin might tease gently but also help Karthik see that nobody is perfect all the time. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense, idealised crush and the first crack in the fantasy.
